title: Winning paths and distant opposition
author: John Bartholomew

source.title: Chess Endgame Fundamentals: King + Pawn vs. King

description: Finish the win from the opposition, defend by keeping the kings on the same file, find Black's only drawing move, and use a reserve tempo.
permissionNote: Lesson for a day of the King and Pawn Endgames course; the course permission (pending) governs it.

chapterData.intro: White just played Kd6: kings on the same file, one square between them, Black to move. Black would love to pass, but he can't. Now finish the job.

chapterData.name: Black to move: take the opposition

children.comment: The defender likes symmetry: kings on the same file, so the white king can't come up. It's a dead draw.
White goes to e4. Find the matching square.
King d6. White can't keep the opposition: he goes to e4 or c4, and Black has a matching square.
Also holds by the engine. John steps straight back, to d6.

chapterData.intro: The same starting position, king on d5 against king and pawn on d2, but Black to move this time. You're Black. What does the opposition tell you?

chapterData.name: Black's only move

children.comment: ...cut back towards the pawn and stay right in front of it.
Also holds by the engine. John cuts back towards the pawn, in front of it.
Also holds by the engine. John cuts back towards the pawn, in front of it.
If White goes too far from the pawn, like Kf3...
King e5, staying in front of the king along the file.
Don't outflank as the defender: White plays Ke4 and you're losing.
Whichever way the white king goes, the defender follows along the file.
Kd5, and Black has taken the opposition. Wherever the white king goes, Black follows.

moves.comment: King e6: the opposition. Same colour squares on the e-file, an odd number of squares between the kings (three this time, distant opposition), and White to move. Whoever breaks the standoff first loses it.
The natural move loses: Kd3 puts Black in zugzwang. Black has to give ground and Kc4 outflanks.
White plays Ke3, and it's the same conclusion: Black has to give ground.
Going to the c-file allows Ke3. The defender shouldn't get into an outflanking race: keep the kings lined up on the file.

chapterData.intro: Change one thing: the black king starts on d6. With White to move it's a draw, because Kd3 meets ...Kd5. With Black to move it's harder: Black has to find an only move. You're Black.

chapterData.name: The reserve tempo

children.comment: Kc5, outflanking, and White will win.
Also wins by the engine, but it gains no ground. Outflank.
Also wins by the engine, but it gains no ground. Outflank.
The opposition depends on whose move it is, so Black isn't happy. Say ...Ke6.
Ke5: the mirror image of Kc5 against ...Ke6.
Also wins by the engine, but it gains no ground. Outflank.
Also wins by the engine, but it gains no ground. Outflank.
If Black leaves d6 the other way, to c6, outflank on the other side.

moves.comment: d3, a reserve tempo. White throws the move back to Black: the king stays on d4, and now Black has to move his.
Also wins by the engine, since the pawn keeps its spare move for later. John spends it now: find the pawn move.

chapterData.intro: An exception. The black king started way back on d8 and took the distant opposition with ...Ke8, five squares between the kings. Then both kings came up: White to d4, Black to d6. It looks like the standoff from the last chapter. What should White do?
